title: Cockchafer soup
lead:
{{Short description|European soup made from insect pests}}
[[File:Maikäfersuppe.jpg|thumb|"Mockchafer soup" made with crab meat in place of cockchafers, and served with toasted bread and liver]]
'''Cockchafer soup''' is a European dish made from the [[cockchafer]] beetle.<ref>Hyman, Vicki (May 29, 2013), "[http://www.nj.com/entertainment/dining/index.ssf/2013/05/cooking_cicadas.html Insect bites: Cooking with cicadas, New Jersey's newest crop] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180710200952/https://www.nj.com/entertainment/dining/index.ssf/2013/05/cooking_cicadas.html |date=2018-07-10 }}." [[NJ.com]]. Retrieved May 31, 2018</ref> Cockchafers were once a common pest insect in Europe, with population explosions every four years.

The origins of cockchafer soup extend back at least as early as 1844, when German medical officer Johann Joseph Schneider reported that in his hometown of [[Fulda]] in [[Hesse]] cockchafers were regularly consumed raw, as well as sugared, candied and in soup. Schneider described the flavour of the soup as similar to crab soup. However, it is unclear how prevalent the consumption of cockchafers including in soup really was (all recipes for cockchafer soup in German are based on Schneider's 1844 version), and it has been suggested that its prevalence has been exaggerated since the 19th century by newspaper stories due to its shocking and sensational nature, leading to it being described as a "myth".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Der Mythos der Maikäfersuppe |trans-title=The myth of cockchafer soup |url=https://campus-a.at/2025/04/25/der-mythos-der-maikafersuppe/ |access-date=2026-03-11 |language=de|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250816043611/https://campus-a.at/2025/04/25/der-mythos-der-maikafersuppe/|url-status=dead|archive-date=16 August 2025}}</ref>

Excessive pesticide usage caused their populations to collapse by the 1970s, with complete [[Local extinction|extirpation]] in many areas.<ref name="r1" />
